questions.title: Example of a secondary cartilaginous joint
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a secondary cartilaginous joint?

explanations.A: Correct. The symphysis pubis is the standard worked example of a secondary cartilaginous joint (a symphysis): the two pubic bones are covered by hyaline cartilage and united across the midline by a pad of fibrocartilage, giving a joint that is slightly mobile rather than fully fixed or freely synovial. Secondary cartilaginous joints characteristically lie in the median plane of the body -- the symphysis pubis and the intervertebral discs are the two classic examples -- which distinguishes them from primary cartilaginous joints (temporary, hyaline-only, growth-plate type) and from the three named fibrous-joint types.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The sternocostal joints (between the costal cartilages and the sternum) are mostly synovial plane joints, not secondary cartilaginous joints.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The costochondral joints (between rib and costal cartilage) are primary cartilaginous joints, a continuous bar of hyaline cartilage with no joint cavity, not secondary cartilaginous ones.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The sacroiliac joint is a synovial joint (with an accessory fibrous component), not a secondary cartilaginous joint.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The sternoclavicular joint is a synovial saddle joint with an intra-articular disc, not a secondary cartilaginous joint.

questions.learning_objective: Name the symphysis pubis as a worked example of a secondary cartilaginous joint.

questions.title: Type of the interphalangeal joints
questions.question: What is the type of the interphalangeal joints?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Condyloid (ellipsoid) describes the metacarpophalangeal and wrist joints, which add abduction/adduction to flexion/extension -- a movement the interphalangeal joints do not have.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Plane describes joints such as the acromioclavicular joint, whose flat surfaces glide on one another, not the interphalangeal joints.
explanations.C: Correct. The interphalangeal joints are synovial hinge joints: uniaxial, permitting flexion and extension only, never abduction, adduction or rotation. This is the same joint-shape classification scheme that places the elbow among the hinge joints and the wrist among the ellipsoid joints -- each named joint of the limb has one shape class, and no two neighbouring joints in the same digit share a type.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pivot describes the superior and inferior radio-ulnar joints, built for rotation (pronation/supination), not the interphalangeal joints.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Saddle describes the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb, not the interphalangeal joints.

questions.learning_objective: Classify the interphalangeal joints as synovial hinge joints.

questions.title: Joint containing a cartilaginous disc
questions.question: What is the joint that contains a cartilaginous disc?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The superior radioulnar joint is a simple synovial pivot joint with no intra-articular disc.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The ankle (talocrural) joint is a synovial hinge joint with no intra-articular disc.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The metacarpophalangeal joints are condyloid synovial joints with no intra-articular disc.
explanations.D: Correct. The temporomandibular joint (TMJ) contains a fibrocartilaginous articular disc that divides its cavity into separate upper and lower synovial compartments, letting the joint combine a hinge-like rotation (lower compartment) with a gliding translation (upper compartment) -- the mechanism behind both simple jaw opening and the fuller protrusive movement of a wide-open mouth. Among the joints listed as options here, only the TMJ is built with this two-compartment, disc-divided design.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The carpometacarpal joint of the thumb is a synovial saddle joint with no intra-articular disc (unlike the sternoclavicular joint, a different saddle joint that does carry one).

questions.learning_objective: Name the temporomandibular joint as the joint containing a fibrocartilaginous articular disc.

questions.title: Most moveable joint type
questions.question: Which one of the following joints is the most moveable?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A suture is a fibrous joint, fixed and essentially immobile until the sutural ligament obliterates with age.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A syndesmosis is a fibrous joint held by an interosseous ligament (as at the inferior tibiofibular joint) -- some give, but far less than a synovial joint.
explanations.C: Correct. Synovial joints are freely mobile, in contrast to fibrous joints (fixed, united by fibrous tissue) and cartilaginous joints (temporary and immobile if primary, slightly mobile if secondary). Hinge is a synovial joint type -- among the five options listed here, it is the only synovial one, and synovial joints as a class permit the greatest range of movement of any joint category.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A gomphosis is a fibrous joint (the periodontal ligament holding a tooth root in its socket), essentially immobile.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A primary cartilaginous joint (such as an epiphyseal growth plate) is temporary and permits no movement at all -- it exists for growth, not mobility.

questions.learning_objective: State that a synovial (e.g. hinge) joint is the most mobile joint category, in contrast to fibrous and cartilaginous joints.

questions.title: Function of the tendon
questions.question: The function of the tendon is to link:

explanations.A: Correct. A tendon is a cord of dense regular connective tissue that attaches a muscle indirectly to bone, transmitting the muscle's pull to its skeletal insertion. This is one of a muscle's three possible modes of attachment -- direct (fibres inserting straight into periosteum), by tendon (a cord, for a concentrated pull), or by aponeurosis (a flattened sheet, for a pull spread over a wide area) -- and it is distinct from a ligament, which instead connects one bone to another rather than muscle to bone.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Linking a bone to a cartilage is not a tendon's role; cartilage-to-bone continuity is how a primary cartilaginous joint (such as a costochondral joint) is built, not a soft-tissue attachment.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A small number of muscles (mostly facial muscles of expression) do insert into skin rather than bone, but this is not the defining function of a tendon in general.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cartilage-to-skin is not a recognised anatomical attachment at all.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Bone-to-bone is the role of a ligament, not a tendon.

questions.learning_objective: State that a tendon links a muscle to a bone.

questions.title: Example of a multipennate muscle
questions.question: Which one of the following muscles is a multipennate muscle?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Flexor pollicis longus is the standard worked example of a unipennate muscle (tendon down one side only), not multipennate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Rectus femoris is the standard worked example of a bipennate muscle (a central tendon with fibres on both sides), not multipennate.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The dorsal interossei are small bipennate hand muscles, not multipennate.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Temporalis is classified by shape as triangular (fan-shaped), a different classification axis from the fibre-direction (pennation) scheme this question tests.
explanations.E: Correct. Deltoid is the standard worked example of a multipennate muscle: several tendinous septa run through its substance, each with fibres attaching obliquely on both sides, like several feathers stacked side by side. Pennation of any degree packs more, shorter fibres into a given muscle volume than a parallel/strap arrangement would, trading range of movement for extra power -- multipennate muscles like deltoid are built for strength across a wide arc, not for a long excursion.

questions.learning_objective: Name deltoid as a worked example of a multipennate muscle.

questions.title: Example of a triangular muscle
questions.question: An example of a triangular muscle is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Sartorius is the standard worked example of a parallel (strap-like) muscle, with fibres running the length of the muscle, not a triangular one.
explanations.B: Correct. Temporalis is a triangular (fan-shaped) muscle: it arises broadly over the temporal fossa and temporal fascia and converges, fan-like, to a narrow insertion by tendon onto the coronoid process and the anterior border of the ramus of the mandible. This shape-based classification (triangular, parallel/strap, and so on) is a separate scheme from the fibre-direction (pennation) classification tested elsewhere in this block -- a muscle's overall outline is triangular here, regardless of how its individual fibres are arranged inside it. The source prints this same correct answer twice under two different option letters (a verbatim duplication in the original scan, not a distinct second distractor); the hand-marked key circles the first occurrence.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Rectus femoris is the standard worked example of a bipennate muscle, not a triangular one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The dorsal interosseous muscles are small bipennate muscles of the hand, not triangular ones.

questions.learning_objective: Name temporalis as a worked example of a triangular (fan-shaped) muscle.

questions.title: Type of the inferior tibiofibular joint
questions.question: Which type of joint is the inferior tibiofibular joint? (matching set: inferior tibiofibular, intervertebral disc, interphalangeal, radioulnar, acromioclavicular)

explanations.A: Incorrect. Plane describes the acromioclavicular joint in this same matching set, not the inferior tibiofibular joint.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hinge describes the interphalangeal joints in this same matching set, not the inferior tibiofibular joint.

explanations.E: Incorrect. Pivot describes the radioulnar joints in this same matching set, not the inferior tibiofibular joint.

questions.title: Type of the intervertebral disc joint
questions.question: Which type of joint is formed at the intervertebral disc? (matching set: inferior tibiofibular, intervertebral disc, interphalangeal, radioulnar, acromioclavicular)

explanations.A: Incorrect. Plane describes the acromioclavicular joint in this same matching set, not the intervertebral disc joint.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hinge describes the interphalangeal joints in this same matching set, not the intervertebral disc joint.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Fibrous describes the inferior tibiofibular joint in this same matching set, not the intervertebral disc joint.
explanations.D: Correct. The joint formed at each intervertebral disc is a secondary cartilaginous joint (a symphysis): the vertebral bodies are covered by hyaline cartilage and united by the fibrocartilaginous disc, giving slight mobility at each level that sums along the whole column into substantial overall spinal movement. Like the symphysis pubis, it lies in the median plane of the body, the characteristic site for secondary cartilaginous joints.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Pivot describes the radioulnar joints in this same matching set, not the intervertebral disc joint.

questions.title: How a secondary cartilaginous joint unites bones
questions.question: The 2ry (secondary) cartilaginous joint unites bones by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Synovial fluid lubricates a synovial joint's cavity; it is not the uniting tissue of a secondary cartilaginous joint.
explanations.B: Correct. A secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis) unites its two bones by a pad of white fibrocartilage, sandwiched between thin layers of hyaline cartilage covering each bone end. The symphysis pubis and the intervertebral discs are the classic examples, and it is this fibrocartilage pad, tougher and slightly compressible, that gives a secondary cartilaginous joint its small amount of give, unlike the rigid hyaline bar of a primary cartilaginous joint.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Fibrous tissue is the uniting material of a fibrous joint (suture, syndesmosis, gomphosis), not a secondary cartilaginous joint.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Yellow elastic cartilage is found in structures such as the pinna of the ear and the epiglottis, not as the uniting tissue of a secondary cartilaginous joint.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Hyaline cartilage alone, with no intervening fibrocartilage and no joint cavity, is what unites the bones at a primary cartilaginous joint, not a secondary one.

questions.learning_objective: State that a secondary cartilaginous joint unites its bones by white fibrocartilage.

questions.title: Joints between the skull vault bones
questions.question: The joints between the bones of the skull vault (cap) belong to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The skull vault joints are not synovial; they are fixed, not freely mobile.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Syndesmosis is a different named type of fibrous joint (bones held by an interosseous ligament, as at the inferior tibiofibular joint), not the type used at the skull vault.
explanations.C: Correct. The joints between the flat bones of the skull vault are sutures, a type of fibrous joint in which the bones are held by a thin sutural ligament. Sutures are fixed and essentially immobile, and the ligament itself obliterates with advancing age, which is why sutures can eventually fuse and disappear as landmarks in old age.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Symphysis (secondary cartilaginous joint) describes joints such as the symphysis pubis and intervertebral discs, not the skull vault.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Gomphosis is the fibrous joint type of a tooth in its socket, not the skull vault.

questions.learning_objective: Classify the skull vault joints as sutures, a type of fibrous joint.

questions.title: Example of a unipennate muscle
questions.question: Which one of the following muscles is a unipennate muscle?

explanations.A: Correct. Flexor pollicis longus is the standard worked example of a unipennate muscle: its tendon runs along one side only, with fibres attaching obliquely to it from the other side, like a single half of a feather. Unipennate is the simplest degree of pennation, in contrast to bipennate (tendon central, fibres on both sides, as in rectus femoris) and multipennate (several tendinous septa, as in deltoid).
explanations.B: Incorrect. Tibialis anterior is described elsewhere in this same bank as a circumpennate muscle, not a unipennate one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The dorsal interosseous muscles are bipennate, not unipennate.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Temporalis is classified by shape as triangular (fan-shaped), a different classification axis from pennation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Deltoid is the standard worked example of a multipennate muscle, not a unipennate one.

questions.learning_objective: Name flexor pollicis longus as a worked example of a unipennate muscle.

questions.title: Which joint is hinge synovial
questions.question: Which one of the following joints is hinge synovial?

explanations.A: Incorrect for this item. The elbow is also a hinge synovial joint (tested as such in a later matching set in this same block), but the option this bank's printed key marks correct here is the interphalangeal joint; both are genuine hinge joints.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The shoulder is a synovial ball-and-socket joint, not a hinge.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The wrist is a synovial ellipsoid (condyloid) joint, not a hinge.
explanations.D: Correct. The interphalangeal joints are synovial hinge joints, uniaxial and limited to flexion and extension. This is the same fact tested twice more elsewhere in this block, once directly ("what is the type of the interphalangeal joints") and once as "which joint is uniaxial". A hinge joint like this one permits no abduction, adduction or rotation at all, which is exactly what separates it from a biaxial joint such as the wrist.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The acromioclavicular joint is a synovial plane joint, not a hinge.

questions.title: Primary cartilaginous joints
questions.question: Primary cartilaginous joints:

options.E: Unite lower ends of tibia & fibula

explanations.A: Correct. Primary cartilaginous joints (synchondroses) are usually temporary: a continuous bar of hyaline cartilage unites the two bony parts, as at an epiphyseal growth plate, and once growth finishes the cartilage itself ossifies and the joint disappears, fusing into a single continuous bone. This temporary, growth-serving nature is what distinguishes a primary cartilaginous joint from a secondary one (permanent, fibrocartilaginous, slightly mobile, e.g. the symphysis pubis).
explanations.B: Incorrect. Primary cartilaginous joints permit no movement at all; they exist for growth, not mobility, unlike freely mobile synovial joints.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The tooth-in-socket joint (gomphosis) is a fibrous joint, not a primary cartilaginous one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Uniting bones by fibrous tissue describes a fibrous joint, not a primary cartilaginous one, which unites by a continuous bar of hyaline cartilage instead.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The lower ends of the tibia and fibula are united at the inferior tibiofibular joint, a fibrous joint (syndesmosis), not a primary cartilaginous one.

questions.learning_objective: State that primary cartilaginous joints are usually temporary, disappearing once growth finishes.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ellipsoid synovial describes joints such as the wrist, not the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hinge synovial describes the elbow in this same matching set, not the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Syndesmosis describes the inferior tibiofibular joint in this same matching set, not the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 1ry cartilaginous describes the epiphyseal plate in this same matching set, not the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb.
explanations.E: Correct. The carpometacarpal joint of the thumb is a synovial saddle joint: its two reciprocally concave-convex surfaces interlock like a rider on a saddle. This gives the thumb its wide range of movement -- flexion, extension, abduction, adduction and, combining these, the opposition that makes the human hand so dexterous. The other named saddle joint in this bank, the sternoclavicular joint, differs in also carrying an intra-articular disc, which this thumb joint does not have.

questions.learning_objective: Classify the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb as a saddle synovial joint.

questions.title: Type of the epiphyseal plate
questions.question: Which type of joint is the epiphyseal plate? (matching set: inferior tibiofibular, carpometacarpal of thumb, elbow, epiphyseal plate)

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ellipsoid synovial describes joints such as the wrist, not the epiphyseal plate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hinge synovial describes the elbow in this same matching set, not the epiphyseal plate.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Syndesmosis describes the inferior tibiofibular joint in this same matching set, not the epiphyseal plate.
explanations.D: Correct. The epiphyseal (growth) plate is a primary cartilaginous joint: a continuous bar of hyaline cartilage between the epiphysis and metaphysis of a growing long bone, permitting no movement and existing purely so the bone can lengthen. Once growth finishes, this cartilage itself ossifies, fusing epiphysis to diaphysis and permanently ending the joint -- the temporary nature that defines primary cartilaginous joints as a class.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Saddle synovial describes the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb in this same matching set, not the epiphyseal plate.

questions.title: Types of muscle attachment, EXCEPT
questions.question: All the following are types of muscle attachments EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this is a genuine muscle attachment type, not the answer). A tendon, a cord of dense connective tissue, is one of the recognised ways a muscle attaches to bone.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this is a genuine muscle attachment type, not the answer). A raphe is a fibrous seam where two muscles (or two halves of one muscle) meet and interdigitate, such as the midline raphe of mylohyoid.
explanations.C: Correct -- this is the exception. A ligament connects one bone to another bone; it is not a form of muscle attachment at all. A muscle attaches to bone directly, or indirectly via a tendon (cord) or an aponeurosis (flattened sheet), or via fleshy fibres inserting straight into periosteum, or via a raphe joining it to another muscle -- ligament plays no role in any of these.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this is a genuine muscle attachment type, not the answer). An aponeurosis, a broad flattened sheet of dense connective tissue, is one of the recognised ways a muscle attaches, spreading its pull over a wide area rather than concentrating it as a tendon does.
explanations.E: Incorrect (i.e. this is a genuine muscle attachment type, not the answer). Fleshy fibres attaching directly into the periosteum, with no intervening tendon or aponeurosis, are a recognised direct form of muscle attachment.

questions.learning_objective: Identify a ligament (bone-to-bone) as not a form of muscle attachment.

questions.title: Muscle producing the opposite action
questions.question: What is the term for a muscle producing the opposite action to a prime mover? (matching set: opposite action, prevents movement of another joint, initiates a movement, aids another in the same movement)

explanations.A: Incorrect. A synergist contracts to cancel unwanted movement at another joint the prime mover crosses, not to oppose the prime mover's own action.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The agonist (prime mover) is the muscle initiating the movement, the opposite role from the one this stem asks about.
explanations.C: Correct. The antagonist is the muscle that opposes the action of the prime mover (agonist) -- for instance, triceps brachii as the antagonist to biceps brachii during elbow flexion. A purposeful movement is never the work of one muscle alone: the antagonist typically relaxes in a controlled way as the agonist contracts, and can reverse the movement by contracting itself once the agonist relaxes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A fixator (stabiliser) fixes the prime mover's origin or stabilises a joint so the prime mover has something to pull against; it does not oppose the prime mover's action.

questions.learning_objective: Name the antagonist as the muscle opposing the prime mover's action.

questions.title: Muscle preventing movement of another joint
questions.question: What is the term for a muscle that fixes or stabilises a joint so another muscle can act on a different joint? (matching set: opposite action, prevents movement of another joint, initiates a movement, aids another in the same movement)

explanations.A: Incorrect. A synergist eliminates unwanted movement at a joint the prime mover itself crosses, a related but distinct role from fixing a separate joint or the prime mover's own origin.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The agonist (prime mover) is the muscle initiating the movement, not the one stabilising a joint so another can act.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The antagonist opposes the prime mover's action; it does not stabilise a joint for another muscle.
explanations.D: Correct. The fixator (stabiliser) fixes the origin of the prime mover, or stabilises the joint on which the prime mover acts, so that the prime mover's pull has a stable base to work against. The muscles that stabilise the scapula so that deltoid can abduct the arm effectively at the shoulder are a worked example of this role. Without a fixator holding the origin still, a prime mover's contraction would simply pull its two ends together rather than moving the intended joint.

questions.learning_objective: Name the fixator as the muscle that stabilises the prime mover's origin or the joint it acts on.

questions.title: Muscle initiating a particular movement
questions.question: What is the term for the muscle initiating a particular movement? (matching set: opposite action, prevents movement of another joint, initiates a movement, aids another in the same movement)

explanations.A: Incorrect. A synergist assists the prime mover indirectly by cancelling unwanted movement elsewhere; it does not itself initiate the movement.
explanations.B: Correct. The agonist, or prime mover, is the muscle that initiates and maintains a given movement -- biceps brachii for elbow flexion is the standard example. Every other role in this four-part scheme is defined relative to the agonist: the antagonist opposes it, the fixator stabilises its origin, and the synergist cleans up its unwanted side effects at other joints.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The antagonist opposes the movement's prime mover; it does not initiate the movement.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A fixator stabilises a joint so the prime mover can act; it does not itself initiate the movement.

questions.title: Muscle aiding another in the same movement
questions.question: What is the term for a muscle that aids another in the same movement by cancelling its unwanted side effects at other joints? (matching set: opposite action, prevents movement of another joint, initiates a movement, aids another in the same movement)

explanations.A: Correct. The synergist contracts to eliminate unwanted movements at the other joints the prime mover crosses, so that the prime mover's action on the joint that actually matters becomes maximal -- for example, the wrist extensors acting as synergists to the long finger flexors, preventing the wrist from flexing as the fingers grip. This is the role most easily confused with the fixator: a fixator holds the prime mover's own origin still, while a synergist cancels the prime mover's own unwanted effect at a joint it crosses on its way to the joint it is meant to act on.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The agonist (prime mover) is the muscle initiating the movement itself, not the one cancelling its side effects elsewhere.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The antagonist opposes the prime mover's action; it does not aid it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A fixator stabilises the prime mover's own origin or the joint it acts on directly, a related but distinct role from cancelling the prime mover's unwanted effect at a different joint it crosses.

questions.learning_objective: Name the synergist as the muscle that cancels the prime mover's unwanted action at another joint it crosses.

questions.title: Example of a parallel type of muscle
questions.question: An example of parallel type of muscle is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Rectus femoris is the standard worked example of a bipennate muscle, not a parallel one.
explanations.B: Correct. Sartorius is the standard worked example of a parallel (strap-like) muscle: its fibres run the whole length of the muscle in the same direction, from origin to insertion, rather than obliquely onto a central tendon as in a pennate muscle. Parallel/strap muscles trade power for range -- their long, unbroken fibres allow a large excursion (fitting for sartorius, the longest muscle in the body, crossing both the hip and knee), unlike a pennate muscle's shorter, more numerous fibres built for force.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The dorsal interosseous muscles are bipennate, not parallel.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Deltoid is the standard worked example of a multipennate muscle, not a parallel one.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Flexor pollicis longus is the standard worked example of a unipennate muscle, not a parallel one.

questions.title: Classification of the symphysis pubis
questions.question: Symphysis pubis is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The symphysis pubis is not synovial at all; it is a cartilaginous joint, not a pivot.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Primary cartilaginous joints are temporary growth-plate-type joints; the symphysis pubis is permanent, so it is a secondary, not primary, cartilaginous joint.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The symphysis pubis is not synovial at all; it is a cartilaginous joint, not a hinge.
explanations.D: Correct. The symphysis pubis is a secondary cartilaginous joint: the two pubic bones, each covered by hyaline cartilage, are united by an interposed pad of white fibrocartilage across the median plane. This is the same fact tested from the opposite direction earlier in this block ("an example of a secondary cartilaginous joint"), and it is the same reasoning that places the intervertebral discs in the same category -- both lie in the median plane, the characteristic site for secondary cartilaginous joints.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A fibrous joint is united by fibrous tissue with no cartilage at all; the symphysis pubis is united by fibrocartilage between cartilage-covered bone ends, which is the cartilaginous, not fibrous, joint category.

questions.learning_objective: Classify the symphysis pubis as a secondary cartilaginous joint.

questions.title: Joint type of most joints in the median plane
questions.question: Most of the joints that lie in the median plane of the body are:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Syndesmosis (a fibrous joint) is exemplified by the inferior tibiofibular joint, a paired limb joint, not a median-plane one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Primary cartilaginous joints (growth plates) occur wherever a long bone is growing, with no particular relationship to the median plane.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Gomphosis (a fibrous joint) is the tooth-in-socket joint, not characteristically a median-plane one.
explanations.D: Correct. Joints lying in the median plane of the body -- the symphysis pubis and the intervertebral discs are the two classic examples -- are typically secondary cartilaginous joints (symphyses), united by fibrocartilage between hyaline-cartilage-covered bone ends and giving slight, summed mobility along the midline. This generalisation is the pattern underlying the two specific median-plane examples tested elsewhere in this block.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Plane synovial joints (such as the acromioclavicular joint) are paired limb-girdle joints, not median-plane ones.

questions.title: Characters of a synovial joint, EXCEPT
questions.question: All are characters of synovial joint EXCEPT:

options.B: A capsule binds its articulating bones
options.D: The articular surfaces are covered by synovial membrane

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this is a genuine synovial-joint character, not the answer). A (potential) joint cavity, holding only a thin film of synovial fluid, is one of the seven named components of every synovial joint.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this is a genuine synovial-joint character, not the answer). A fibrous capsule surrounding the joint and binding its articulating bones, strengthened by ligaments, is a genuine component of a synovial joint.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this is a genuine synovial-joint character, not the answer). Some synovial joints (such as the sternoclavicular or temporomandibular joints, or the knee's menisci) do contain an intra-articular disc or meniscus.
explanations.D: Correct -- this is the exception. The articular surfaces of a synovial joint are covered by hyaline articular cartilage, not by synovial membrane. The synovial membrane instead lines everything inside the joint capsule except the articular surfaces themselves, and it is this membrane that secretes and absorbs the synovial fluid. Confusing the two coverings is a common error, since both line the same joint cavity but over different, mutually exclusive surfaces of it.
explanations.E: Incorrect (i.e. this is a genuine synovial-joint character, not the answer). Synovial joints are freely mobile, in contrast to fibrous and cartilaginous joints -- the same fact tested from a different angle elsewhere in this block ("which one of the following joints is the most moveable").

questions.learning_objective: Identify that a synovial joint's articular surfaces are covered by hyaline cartilage, not by synovial membrane.

questions.title: Cartilaginous joints, INCORRECT statement
questions.question: As regards the cartilaginous joints, choose the INCORRECT statement:

options.A: Secondary cartilaginous joints allow limited movement
options.B: Syndesmosis is a type of primary cartilaginous joint
options.C: Primary cartilaginous joints are usually temporary
options.D: Secondary cartilaginous joints lie usually in median plane

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). Secondary cartilaginous joints do allow a limited amount of movement -- the small give at the symphysis pubis or between vertebrae, summed along the whole spine, is exactly this limited mobility.
explanations.B: Correct -- this is the incorrect statement. Syndesmosis is not a type of primary cartilaginous joint at all; it is one of the three named types of fibrous joint (alongside gomphosis and suture), exemplified by the inferior tibiofibular joint, where bones are held by an interosseous ligament. This is the false pairing the question is built to catch, and it directly contradicts this block's own repeated classification of the inferior tibiofibular joint as fibrous/syndesmosis elsewhere.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). Primary cartilaginous joints are indeed usually temporary, disappearing once the cartilage ossifies at the end of growth -- the same fact tested directly elsewhere in this block.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). Secondary cartilaginous joints do usually lie in the median plane of the body, as the symphysis pubis and intervertebral discs illustrate -- the same generalisation tested directly elsewhere in this block.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that syndesmosis is a type of fibrous joint, not a type of primary cartilaginous joint.

questions.title: Primary cartilaginous joints, second statement
questions.question: Primary cartilaginous joints:

options.D: Unite lower end of tibia & fibula
options.E: Occur between the tooth & socket in the jaw

explanations.A: Incorrect. Primary cartilaginous joints permit no movement at all, unlike freely mobile synovial joints.
explanations.B: Correct. Primary cartilaginous joints usually ossify with age: the continuous bar of hyaline cartilage that forms the joint (as at an epiphyseal growth plate) is itself gradually replaced by bone once growth is complete, fusing the two parts into one continuous bone and ending the joint altogether. This is the mechanism behind this same class's temporary nature, tested from the angle of duration elsewhere in this block.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Uniting the two pubic bones is the symphysis pubis, a secondary cartilaginous joint, not a primary one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Uniting the lower ends of the tibia and fibula is the inferior tibiofibular joint, a fibrous joint (syndesmosis), not a primary cartilaginous one.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The tooth-in-socket joint (gomphosis) is a fibrous joint, not a primary cartilaginous one.

questions.title: Muscles, INCORRECT statement (first)
questions.question: As regards the muscles, choose the INCORRECT statement:

options.A: A bipennate muscle looks like a complete feather
options.B: The most movemable part of the muscle is its origin
options.C: A raphe is a mixture of fleshy & tendinous fibers
options.D: The muscle may be inserted into the skin
options.E: Most muscles have tendons attached to bones

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). A bipennate muscle does look like a complete feather -- its central tendon is the shaft, with fibres set obliquely on both sides like the barbs, unlike a unipennate muscle's tendon-on-one-side arrangement, which resembles only half a feather.
explanations.B: Correct -- this is the incorrect statement. The origin is conventionally the more fixed end of a muscle's two attachments, not the most movable one. The insertion is the end that moves, since it is the origin that is stabilised (often by a fixator muscle) so the muscle's pull can act on the insertion. The same reversed-convention error is tested again from the opposite phrasing later in this block, as "the origin is the most moveable end of the muscle".
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). A raphe is indeed a fibrous seam of mixed fleshy and tendinous fibres where two muscles, or two halves of one muscle, meet and interdigitate.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). Some muscles (mostly facial muscles of expression) do insert into the skin rather than into bone.
explanations.E: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). Most skeletal muscles do have tendons attaching them to bones, one of the three recognised modes of muscle attachment.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that the origin, not the insertion, is conventionally the fixed end of a muscle.

questions.title: Skeletal muscles, INCORRECT statement
questions.question: As regards the skeletal muscles, choose the INCORRECT statement:

options.A: The origin is the most moveable end of the muscle
options.B: Contraction means approximation of origin & insertion
options.C: Septa from deep fascia divide them into groups
options.D: They are mostly under voluntary control
options.E: They are innervated by motor, sensory & autonomic nerve fibers

explanations.A: Correct -- this is the incorrect statement. The origin is conventionally the fixed, not the most movable, end of a muscle. The insertion is the end that moves as the muscle contracts, drawing toward the stabilised origin. This is the same reversed-convention error tested from the opposite phrasing earlier in this block ("the most movable part of the muscle is its origin").
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). Muscle contraction does mean approximation of origin and insertion, drawing the two attachment points closer together, which is the basic mechanical definition of what a contracting muscle does.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). Septa extending inward from the deep fascia do divide skeletal muscles into compartments/groups, such as the anterior and posterior compartments of the limbs.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). Skeletal muscles are indeed mostly under voluntary control, in contrast to smooth and cardiac muscle.
explanations.E: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). Skeletal muscles are innervated by motor fibres (to their fibres), sensory fibres (from their proprioceptors, such as muscle spindles) and autonomic fibres (to their blood vessels).
